title: The Changing World of Work: Careers in the 21st Century
paragraphs: The concept of a "career" has changed dramatically over the past generation. For much of the twentieth century, the dominant model was the "organisational career" — a person joined a company or institution in their twenties, worked their way up through a defined hierarchy, and retired with a pension after thirty or forty years. This model offered security, predictability, and a clear sense of progression. It also offered, for many workers, a sense of identity: you were your job, your employer, your professional role.

This model has largely broken down. The average person in a developed country today changes jobs every four to five years, and many people change careers — not just employers — multiple times over their working lives. The causes of this shift are multiple: the decline of large, stable employers in manufacturing and the public sector; the rise of a more fluid labour market in which skills and projects matter more than institutional loyalty; and the growing expectation, particularly among younger workers, that work should be personally meaningful and not merely financially adequate.

The gig economy represents one of the most significant developments in this transformation. Platforms like Uber, Deliveroo, and Upwork have created a large class of workers who are formally self-employed but who depend on a single platform for most of their income. For some, this offers genuine flexibility and autonomy. For others, it means the worst of both worlds: the insecurity of self-employment without the independence, and the dependency of employment without the rights. The legal and regulatory debate about how to classify and protect gig workers remains unresolved in most countries.

Remote work — working from home or from locations other than a central office — was transformed by the COVID-19 pandemic from a rare privilege to a widespread practice, almost overnight. For many workers, particularly those in knowledge-intensive roles, this change was broadly positive: it eliminated commuting, increased flexibility, and demonstrated that productivity did not require physical co-presence. For others — those in roles that require collaboration, equipment, or physical presence — the transition was much harder. And for workers without stable housing or adequate home working conditions, remote work was simply not an option.

The rise of automation and artificial intelligence is creating new uncertainties about the future of specific roles and entire occupational categories. While new jobs will certainly be created, the transition will not be smooth or equal. Workers in routine cognitive roles — data entry, basic accounting, customer service, legal research — are at the greatest risk. Workers in roles requiring creativity, complex human interaction, ethical judgement, and physical dexterity are likely to be more resilient. But resilience is not immunity: almost every role will be changed, even if not eliminated.

Against this backdrop of uncertainty, the concept of "career capital" has gained importance. Career capital refers to the skills, knowledge, experience, and relationships that make a person valuable in the labour market — and that they carry with them across jobs and employers. Building career capital requires deliberate investment: seeking out challenging assignments, developing expertise in areas of genuine demand, maintaining professional networks, and continuously updating skills. The individual who treats their career as a passive recipient of what employers offer will find themselves vulnerable; the one who actively manages it as a portfolio of developing assets will be more resilient.

Ambition — the desire to achieve, to progress, to matter — remains a powerful driver of career decisions. But ambition itself is changing. Younger workers increasingly express ambition not just in terms of money and status, but in terms of purpose, impact, and work-life integration. They want to do work that contributes to something larger than the organisation's profit margin, and they want organisations that respect the full humanity of the people who work for them. Whether this represents a genuine cultural shift or a temporary product of economic circumstances remains to be seen — but it is reshaping the expectations that employers must meet.
